claim: The human macula is more susceptible than the peripheral retina to developing age-related macular degeneration.
source: The human macula is more susceptible than the peripheral retina to developing blinding conditions such as age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about macular susceptibility to disease.

claim: The human macula is more susceptible than the peripheral retina to developing diabetic retinopathy.
source: The human macula is more susceptible than the peripheral retina to developing blinding conditions such as age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about macular susceptibility to disease.

claim: Primary cultured Müller cells from macula and peripheral retina display significant morphological differences.
source: We found primary cultured Müller cells from macula and peripheral retina display significant morphological and transcriptomic differences.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations described in the abstract and detailed in Figure 1.

claim: Primary cultured Müller cells from macula and peripheral retina display significant transcriptomic differences.
source: We found primary cultured Müller cells from macula and peripheral retina display significant morphological and transcriptomic differences.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Macular Müller cells expressed more phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH) than peripheral Müller cells.
source: Macular Müller cells expressed more phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH, a rate-limiting enzyme in serine synthesis) than peripheral Müller cells.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: PHGDH is a rate-limiting enzyme in serine synthesis.
source: Macular Müller cells expressed more phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH, a rate-limiting enzyme in serine synthesis) than peripheral Müller cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PHGDH function.

claim: Serine synthesis was more activated in macular than peripheral Müller cells.
source: The serine synthesis, glycolytic and mitochondrial function were more activated in macular than peripheral Müller cells.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose labeling experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Glycolytic function was more activated in macular than peripheral Müller cells.
source: The serine synthesis, glycolytic and mitochondrial function were more activated in macular than peripheral Müller cells.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse XF analysis shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Mitochondrial function was more activated in macular than peripheral Müller cells.
source: The serine synthesis, glycolytic and mitochondrial function were more activated in macular than peripheral Müller cells.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse XF analysis shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: Serine biosynthesis is critical in defending against oxidative stress.
source: Serine biosynthesis is critical in defending against oxidative stress.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental results with PHGDH inhibition.

claim: Intracellular reactive oxygen species levels were increased in primary cultured macular Müller cells.
source: Intracellular reactive oxygen species and glutathione levels were increased in primary cultured macular Müller cells which were more susceptible to oxidative stress after inhibition of PHGDH.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6G-I.

claim: Intracellular glutathione levels were increased in primary cultured macular Müller cells.
source: Intracellular reactive oxygen species and glutathione levels were increased in primary cultured macular Müller cells which were more susceptible to oxidative stress after inhibition of PHGDH.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Macular Müller cells were more susceptible to oxidative stress after inhibition of PHGDH.
source: Intracellular reactive oxygen species and glutathione levels were increased in primary cultured macular Müller cells which were more susceptible to oxidative stress after inhibition of PHGDH.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability and cytotoxicity assays shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: Serine biosynthesis is a critical part of the macular defence against oxidative stress.
source: Our findings indicate serine biosynthesis is a critical part of the macular defence against oxidative stress and suggest dysregulation of this pathway as a potential cause of macular pathology.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing increased susceptibility to oxidative stress when PHGDH is inhibited.

claim: Dysregulation of serine biosynthesis is a potential cause of macular pathology.
source: Our findings indicate serine biosynthesis is a critical part of the macular defence against oxidative stress and suggest dysregulation of this pathway as a potential cause of macular pathology.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental findings and their implications for disease.

claim: The macula is a specialized region located at the posterior pole of the primate retina.
source: The macula, a specialized region located at the posterior pole of the primate retina, has the greatest density of cone photoreceptors for the highest visual acuity (Sharon et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge cited from Sharon et al., 2002.

claim: The macula has the greatest density of cone photoreceptors for the highest visual acuity.
source: The macula, a specialized region located at the posterior pole of the primate retina, has the greatest density of cone photoreceptors for the highest visual acuity (Sharon et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge cited from Sharon et al., 2002.

claim: The macula occupies less than 1.4% of the retina area.
source: Although the macula occupies less than 1.4% of the retina area, it contains ~8.4% of cones,~3.4% of rods and ~60% of the ganglion cells (Curcio and Allen, 1990).
evidence: This is cited from Curcio and Allen, 1990.

claim: The macula contains approximately 8.4% of cones.
source: Although the macula occupies less than 1.4% of the retina area, it contains ~8.4% of cones,~3.4% of rods and ~60% of the ganglion cells (Curcio and Allen, 1990).
evidence: This is cited from Curcio and Allen, 1990.

claim: The macula contains approximately 3.4% of rods.
source: Although the macula occupies less than 1.4% of the retina area, it contains ~8.4% of cones,~3.4% of rods and ~60% of the ganglion cells (Curcio and Allen, 1990).
evidence: This is cited from Curcio and Allen, 1990.

claim: The macula contains approximately 60% of the ganglion cells.
source: Although the macula occupies less than 1.4% of the retina area, it contains ~8.4% of cones,~3.4% of rods and ~60% of the ganglion cells (Curcio and Allen, 1990).
evidence: This is cited from Curcio and Allen, 1990.

claim: The ratio of cones to rods is 1:8 in the macula.
source: The ratio of cones to rods is much higher in the macula (1:8) than that in the peripheral retina (1:20) (Curcio et al., 1990).
evidence: This is cited from Curcio et al., 1990.

claim: The ratio of cones to rods is 1:20 in the peripheral retina.
source: The ratio of cones to rods is much higher in the macula (1:8) than that in the peripheral retina (1:20) (Curcio et al., 1990).
evidence: This is cited from Curcio et al., 1990.

claim: The high density of neurons in the macula is associated with a high metabolic rate.
source: The high density of neurons in the macula is associated with a high metabolic rate and increased levels of oxidative stress (Handa, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Handa, 2012.

claim: The high density of neurons in the macula is associated with increased levels of oxidative stress.
source: The high density of neurons in the macula is associated with a high metabolic rate and increased levels of oxidative stress (Handa, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Handa, 2012.

claim: Müller cells are the major glial cells of retina.
source: Müller cells, the major glial cells of retina, are responsible for retinal redox homeostasis and metabolic support of retinal neurons (Reichenbach and Bringmann, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Reichenbach and Bringmann, 2013.

claim: Müller cells are responsible for retinal redox homeostasis.
source: Müller cells, the major glial cells of retina, are responsible for retinal redox homeostasis and metabolic support of retinal neurons (Reichenbach and Bringmann, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Reichenbach and Bringmann, 2013.

claim: Müller cells are responsible for metabolic support of retinal neurons.
source: Müller cells, the major glial cells of retina, are responsible for retinal redox homeostasis and metabolic support of retinal neurons (Reichenbach and Bringmann, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Reichenbach and Bringmann, 2013.

claim: Müller cells control the composition of retinal extracellular fluids by mediating the transcellular transport of ions, water and bicarbonate.
source: They control the composition of retinal extracellular fluids by mediating the transcellular transport of ions, water and bicarbonate (Bringmann et al., 2005; Kofuji and Newman, 2004; Newman, 1996).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources: Bringmann et al., 2005; Kofuji and Newman, 2004; Newman, 1996.

claim: Müller cells may play an important role in retinal glucose metabolism.
source: They may play an important role in retinal glucose metabolism and provide substrates to photoreceptors, one of the most metabolically active cell types in the body (Poitry-Yamate et al., 1995).
evidence: This is cited from Poitry-Yamate et al., 1995.

claim: Müller cells provide substrates to photoreceptors.
source: They may play an important role in retinal glucose metabolism and provide substrates to photoreceptors, one of the most metabolically active cell types in the body (Poitry-Yamate et al., 1995).
evidence: This is cited from Poitry-Yamate et al., 1995.

claim: Photoreceptors are one of the most metabolically active cell types in the body.
source: They may play an important role in retinal glucose metabolism and provide substrates to photoreceptors, one of the most metabolically active cell types in the body (Poitry-Yamate et al., 1995).
evidence: This is cited from Poitry-Yamate et al., 1995.

claim: Müller cells promote photoreceptor survival by providing neurotrophic substances.
source: Müller cells also promote photoreceptor survival by providing neurotrophic substances and removing metabolic end products (Poitry et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from Poitry et al., 2000.

claim: Müller cells promote photoreceptor survival by removing metabolic end products.
source: Müller cells also promote photoreceptor survival by providing neurotrophic substances and removing metabolic end products (Poitry et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from Poitry et al., 2000.

claim: Foveal Müller cells are Z-shaped.
source: Foveal Müller cells are Z-shaped: their processes run vertically from the inner limiting membrane (ILM) to the inner nuclear layer (INL), then horizontally away from the fovea within Henle's fibre layer (HFL) then vertically again to the outer limiting membrane (OLM).
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge about foveal Müller cell morphology.

claim: Müller cells from the macula and the periphery both express CD117.
source: Müller cells from the macula and the periphery both express CD117 but only peripheral Müller cells express CD44 (Too et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Too et al., 2017.

claim: Only peripheral Müller cells express CD44.
source: Müller cells from the macula and the periphery both express CD117 but only peripheral Müller cells express CD44 (Too et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Too et al., 2017.

claim: Macular Müller cells express more Aquaporin-4 than peripheral Müller cells.
source: Macular Müller cells also express more Aquaporin-4 than peripheral Müller cells, which may contribute to a specialized 'glymphatic system' of the macula (Daruich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Daruich et al., 2018.

claim: Müller cell dysfunction has been implicated in macular telangiectasia type 2.
source: Müller cell dysfunction has been implicated in MacTel) (Powner et al., 2010) and in a form of autoimmune retinopathy (Peek et al., 1998).
evidence: This is cited from Powner et al., 2010.

claim: Müller cell dysfunction has been implicated in a form of autoimmune retinopathy.
source: Müller cell dysfunction has been implicated in MacTel) (Powner et al., 2010) and in a form of autoimmune retinopathy (Peek et al., 1998).
evidence: This is cited from Peek et al., 1998.

claim: Müller cells are the major sites in the retina of de novo synthesis of serine.
source: Recent report suggests that Müller cells are the major sites in the retina of de novo synthesis of serine and glutathione which support retinal neurons and protect them from oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Müller cells are the major sites in the retina of de novo synthesis of glutathione.
source: Recent report suggests that Müller cells are the major sites in the retina of de novo synthesis of serine and glutathione which support retinal neurons and protect them from oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: M-huPMCs were small, spindle- or stellate-shaped cells with a low cytoplasm/nucleus ratio.
source: M-huPMCs were small, spindle- or stellate-shaped cells with a low cytoplasm/nucleus ratio (Figure 1B & C)
evidence: This is supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: P-huPMCs had large cell bodies, multiple cytoplasmic processes and a higher cytoplasm/nucleus ratio.
source: the P-huPMCs had large cell bodies, multiple cytoplasmic processes and a higher cytoplasm/nucleus ratio (Figure 1B & E).
evidence: This is supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 1B and E.

claim: Both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs without sub-culturing (P0) demonstrated positive immunolabeling for GFAP.
source: Both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs without sub-culturing (P0) demonstrated positive immunolabeling for four Müller-cell-specific markers: Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) (Figure 1G–H)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: Both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs without sub-culturing (P0) demonstrated positive immunolabeling for carbonic anhydrase II.
source: Both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs without sub-culturing (P0) demonstrated positive immunolabeling for four Müller-cell-specific markers: Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) (Figure 1G–H), carbonic anhydrase II (Figure 1I–J)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1I-J.

claim: Both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs without sub-culturing (P0) demonstrated positive immunolabeling for SOX9.
source: Both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs without sub-culturing (P0) demonstrated positive immunolabeling for four Müller-cell-specific markers: Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) (Figure 1G–H), carbonic anhydrase II (Figure 1I–J), SOX9 (Figure 1K–L) (Song et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1K-L.

claim: Both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs without sub-culturing (P0) demonstrated positive immunolabeling for CRALBP.
source: Both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs without sub-culturing (P0) demonstrated positive immunolabeling for four Müller-cell-specific markers: Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) (Figure 1G–H), carbonic anhydrase II (Figure 1I–J), SOX9 (Figure 1K–L) (Song et al., 2013) and Cellular Retinaldehyde Binding Protein (CRALBP) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A total of 7588 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified in Müller cells isolated from human macula and peripheral retina with a 1.5-fold or more increase or decrease and with an FDR corrected p-value<0.05.
source: A total of 7588 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified in Müller cells isolated from human macula and peripheral retina with a 1.5-fold or more increase or decrease and with an FDR corrected p-value<0.05 (Figure 2F, Supplementary S1 and S2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2F and supplementary data.

claim: Upregulated genes in M-huPMCs were significantly associated with 'response to oxygen levels'.
source: Based on gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis (ClusterProfiler), these upregulated genes were significantly associated with numerous GO Biological process terms, including 'response to oxygen levels', 'response to decreased oxygen levels' and 'response to hypoxia' (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Upregulated genes in M-huPMCs were significantly associated with 'response to decreased oxygen levels'.
source: Based on gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis (ClusterProfiler), these upregulated genes were significantly associated with numerous GO Biological process terms, including 'response to oxygen levels', 'response to decreased oxygen levels' and 'response to hypoxia' (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Upregulated genes in M-huPMCs were significantly associated with 'response to hypoxia'.
source: Based on gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis (ClusterProfiler), these upregulated genes were significantly associated with numerous GO Biological process terms, including 'response to oxygen levels', 'response to decreased oxygen levels' and 'response to hypoxia' (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs strongly expressed vimentin.
source: RNA sequencing found that both the M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs strongly expressed (high RPKM number [Reads Per Kilobase of transcript per Million mapped reads]) gene markers for the Müller cell: vimentin, glutamine synthetase (GS), CRALBP, clusterin, carbonic anhydrase II and GFAP (Table 1)
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Table 1.

claim: Both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs strongly expressed glutamine synthetase.
source: RNA sequencing found that both the M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs strongly expressed (high RPKM number [Reads Per Kilobase of transcript per Million mapped reads]) gene markers for the Müller cell: vimentin, glutamine synthetase (GS), CRALBP, clusterin, carbonic anhydrase II and GFAP (Table 1)
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Table 1.

claim: Both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs negligibly expressed rhodopsin.
source: and negligibly expression (low RPKM number) of gene markers of the other retinal cell types: rhodopsin for photoreceptors; mGluR6 for the bipolar cells, syntaxin 1A for the amacrine cells, Iba1 for the microglia cells and PECAM1 for vascular endothelial cells (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Table 1.

claim: The expression of Müller cell markers was higher in the P-huPMCs compared to M-huPMCs.
source: Notably, the expression of Müller cell markers was higher in the P-huPMCs compared to M-huPMCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data presented in Table 1.

claim: The expression of key genes related to de novo serine synthesis (e.g. PHGDH, PSAT1 and SHMT2) was higher in M-huPMCs than in P-huPMCs.
source: We found in the present study that the expression of key genes related to de novo serine synthesis (e.g. PHGDH, PSAT1 and SHMT2) was higher in M-huPMCs than in P-huPMCs (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Table 2.

claim: M-huPMCs expressed significantly more PHGDH compared to P-huPMCs.
source: Western blot studies found that M-huPMCs expressed significantly more PHGDH compared to P-huPMCs (Figure 3A–B, normalized to β-actin, n = 4 donor retinas).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Macula expressed significantly more PHGDH than punches from the peripheral retina.
source: We found that macula expressed significantly more PHGDH (Figure 3D–F, normalized to α/β-Tubulin or Figure 3—figure supplement 1, normalized to total loaded retinal protein) than punches from the peripheral retina, although there were inter-individual variations between the five retinas.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PHGDH expression from the retina largely reflects its expression by Müller cells since they are the main source of PHGDH in the human retina.
source: We believe that PHGDH expression from the retina largely reflects its expression by Müller cells since they are the main source of PHGDH in the human retina (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred based on previous findings cited from Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: PHGDH in the retina is predominantly expressed in the Müller cells.
source: This is consistent with our previous study that PHGDH in the retina is predominantly expressed in the Müller cells(Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: The macula has multiple layers of Müller cell nuclei in the inner nuclear layer.
source: In contrast to the peripheral retina (Figure 4M–P), the macula has multiple layers of Müller cell nuclei in the inner nuclear layer and strongly expresses PHGDH in Henle fibre layer (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E-H.

claim: The macula strongly expresses PHGDH in Henle fibre layer.
source: In contrast to the peripheral retina (Figure 4M–P), the macula has multiple layers of Müller cell nuclei in the inner nuclear layer and strongly expresses PHGDH in Henle fibre layer (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E-H.

claim: After 3 hr labeling, around 18% of cellular serine was replaced by 13C-glucose.
source: After 3 hr labeling, around 18% of cellular serine (average of both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs) was replaced by 13C-glucose (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose labeling experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: M-huPMCs had higher 13C labelled serine (24%) than P-huPMCs (13%).
source: M-huPMCs had higher 13C labelled serine (24%) and 13C-labeled glycine (12%) than of P-huPMCs (13% and 5% respectively, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose labeling experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: M-huPMCs had higher 13C-labeled glycine (12%) than P-huPMCs (5%).
source: M-huPMCs had higher 13C labelled serine (24%) and 13C-labeled glycine (12%) than of P-huPMCs (13% and 5% respectively, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose labeling experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: M-huPMCs had significantly higher glycolytic capacity than P-huPMCs.
source: We found that M-huPMCs had significantly higher glycolytic capacity and reserve than P-huPMCs (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse XF analysis shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: M-huPMCs had significantly higher glycolytic reserve than P-huPMCs.
source: We found that M-huPMCs had significantly higher glycolytic capacity and reserve than P-huPMCs (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse XF analysis shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: M-huPMCs had significantly higher basal mitochondrial respiration than P-huPMCs.
source: M-huPMCs also had significantly higher basal mitochondrial respiration and ATP production but lower spare respiratory capacity than P-huPMCs (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse XF analysis shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: M-huPMCs had significantly higher ATP production than P-huPMCs.
source: M-huPMCs also had significantly higher basal mitochondrial respiration and ATP production but lower spare respiratory capacity than P-huPMCs (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse XF analysis shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: M-huPMCs had lower spare respiratory capacity than P-huPMCs.
source: M-huPMCs also had significantly higher basal mitochondrial respiration and ATP production but lower spare respiratory capacity than P-huPMCs (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse XF analysis shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: Treatment of CBR-5884 in huPMCs for 2 hr resulted in 61% reduction in serine levels.
source: We first validated the inhibition efficiency of CBR-5884 in human primary Müller cells and found that treatment of CBR-5884 in huPMCs for 2 hr resulted in 61% and 42% reductions in serine and glycine levels, respectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Treatment of CBR-5884 in huPMCs for 2 hr resulted in 42% reduction in glycine levels.
source: We first validated the inhibition efficiency of CBR-5884 in human primary Müller cells and found that treatment of CBR-5884 in huPMCs for 2 hr resulted in 61% and 42% reductions in serine and glycine levels, respectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: M-huPMCs had significantly lower cell viability than P-huPMCs when they were exposed to exogenous oxidative stress (100 µM H2O2).
source: M-huPMCs had significantly lower cell viability and higher cytotoxicity levels than P-huPMCs when they were exposed to exogenous oxidative stress (100 µM H2O2) (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: M-huPMCs had significantly higher cytotoxicity levels than P-huPMCs when they were exposed to exogenous oxidative stress (100 µM H2O2).
source: M-huPMCs had significantly lower cell viability and higher cytotoxicity levels than P-huPMCs when they were exposed to exogenous oxidative stress (100 µM H2O2) (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Inhibiting PHGDH using CBR-5884 when cells were exposed to oxidative stress led to more pronounced Müller cells cytotoxicity in the macula compared to the periphery.
source: Inhibiting PHGDH using CBR-5884 when cells were exposed to oxidative stress led to more pronounced Müller cells cytotoxicity in the macula compared to the periphery.
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: M-huPMCs had significantly higher intracellular levels of GSH than P-huPMCs.
source: We found significantly higher intracellular levels of GSH in M-huPMCs than in P-huPMCs (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: When cells were subjected to mild oxidative stress (100 μM H2O2), P-huPMCs had a more pronounced decrease of GSH levels than M-huPMCs.
source: When the cells were also subjected to mild oxidative stress (100 μM H2O2), P-huPMCs had a more pronounced decrease of GSH levels and elevated ROS levels than M-huPMCs.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: When cells were subjected to mild oxidative stress (100 μM H2O2), P-huPMCs had elevated ROS levels compared to M-huPMCs.
source: When the cells were also subjected to mild oxidative stress (100 μM H2O2), P-huPMCs had a more pronounced decrease of GSH levels and elevated ROS levels than M-huPMCs.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Inhibition of PHGDH using CBR-5884 induced a more significant GSH reduction in M-huPMCs than in P-huPMCs.
source: Inhibition of PHGDH using CBR-5884 induced a more significant GSH reduction in M-huPMCs than in P-huPMCs; ROS levels significantly increased in both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs (Figure 6F–I, normalized to control of P-huPMCs or Figure 6—figure supplement 1, normalized to P-huPMCs/M-huPMCs own control).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Inhibition of PHGDH using CBR-5884 significantly increased ROS levels in both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs.
source: Inhibition of PHGDH using CBR-5884 induced a more significant GSH reduction in M-huPMCs than in P-huPMCs; ROS levels significantly increased in both M-huPMCs and P-huPMCs (Figure 6F–I, normalized to control of P-huPMCs or Figure 6—figure supplement 1, normalized to P-huPMCs/M-huPMCs own control).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Müller cells isolated from macula were small spindle to stellate shaped cells with lower cytoplasm/nucleus ratios and shorter processes in culture.
source: In culture, we found that Müller cells isolated from macula were small spindle to stellate shaped cells with lower cytoplasm/nucleus ratios and shorter processes, while the Müller cells from peripheral retina had larger cell bodies, multiple cytoplasmic processes, higher cytoplasm/nucleus ratios.
evidence: This is supported by morphological observations described in the Results section.

claim: Müller cells from peripheral retina had larger cell bodies, multiple cytoplasmic processes, higher cytoplasm/nucleus ratios in culture.
source: In culture, we found that Müller cells isolated from macula were small spindle to stellate shaped cells with lower cytoplasm/nucleus ratios and shorter processes, while the Müller cells from peripheral retina had larger cell bodies, multiple cytoplasmic processes, higher cytoplasm/nucleus ratios.
evidence: This is supported by morphological observations described in the Results section.

claim: These phenotypic differences were retained in the two sub-populations of Müller cells up to the second passage (P2).
source: These phenotypic differences were retained in the two sub-populations of Müller cells up to the second passage (P2), after which cells showed evidence of division more towards immortalized 'MIO-M1'-shaped cells.
evidence: This is based on observations of cell morphology over multiple passages.

claim: Peripheral Müller cells expressed Müller cell markers more strongly than those from the macula.
source: Interestingly, peripheral Müller cells expressed Müller cell markers more strongly than those from the macula, perhaps in keeping with their ability to maintain a more 'Müller-like' morphology in primary culture.
evidence: This is inferred from RNA-seq data and morphological observations.

claim: Human Müller cells from the macula expressed less GS than those from the retinal periphery.
source: It has been reported that human Müller cells from the macula expressed less GS than those from the retinal periphery (Daruich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Daruich et al., 2018.

claim: De novo serine synthesis plays important roles in Müller cellular redox homeostasis.
source: We have previously reported that de novo serine synthesis plays important roles in Müller cellular redox homeostasis and mitochondrial function (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: De novo serine synthesis plays important roles in Müller cellular mitochondrial function.
source: We have previously reported that de novo serine synthesis plays important roles in Müller cellular redox homeostasis and mitochondrial function (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: The strong expression of PHGDH in Henle's fibre layer may explain why macular Müller cells express more PHGDH than those from the retinal periphery.
source: The strong expression of PHGDH in Henle's fibre layer, a specialised region of the macula, may explain why macular Müller cells express more PHGDH than those from the retinal periphery.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing PHGDH expression patterns.

claim: The macula has the highest metabolic activity in the retina related to the very high density of neurons, especially cone photoreceptors within the fovea.
source: The macula has the highest metabolic activity in the retina related to the very high density of neurons, especially cone photoreceptors within the fovea (Okawa et al., 2008; Perkins et al., 2004; Perkins and Frey, 2000).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources: Okawa et al., 2008; Perkins et al., 2004; Perkins and Frey, 2000.

claim: Human macular Müller cells display a more active glycolytic metabolism than peripheral Müller cells.
source: As the major supporting glial cell in the retina, it is not surprising that human macular Müller cells display a more active glycolytic and mitochondrial metabolism than peripheral Müller cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the Seahorse XF experimental results.

claim: Human macular Müller cells display a more active mitochondrial metabolism than peripheral Müller cells.
source: As the major supporting glial cell in the retina, it is not surprising that human macular Müller cells display a more active glycolytic and mitochondrial metabolism than peripheral Müller cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the Seahorse XF experimental results.

claim: Müller cells in primary cell culture had very high de novo serine/glycine enrichment (around 18% within 3 hr).
source: Studies using C13-glucose tracer revealed that Müller cells in primary cell culture had very high de novo serine/glycine enrichment (around 18% within 3 hr), much higher than those reported for melanoma cells, where only around 12% of serine was labeled with C13-glucose within 24 hr (Scott et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose labeling experiments and compared to literature values.

claim: In melanoma cells, only around 12% of serine was labeled with C13-glucose within 24 hr.
